questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to cook octopus at home
How clever octopuses manage to escape from aquariums
Whether it is right to farm octopus for food
Why octopus populations are falling
questions.why: Beth says they'll discuss whether farming octopus can ever be ethical.

questions.q: What does Beth admit she thinks about when she hears the word “octopus”?
options: How good they taste
How dangerous they are
How ugly they look
How rare they are
questions.why: She mentions their intelligence, but admits she also thinks about how they taste – delicious.

questions.q: Where is octopus most commonly eaten?
options: Britain, France, Germany and the Netherlands
New Zealand and Australia
Mexico and the USA
South Korea, Spain, Portugal and Japan
questions.why: Neil lists South Korea, Spain, Portugal and Japan.

questions.q: Why do campaigners object to farming octopus?
options: Farmed octopus doesn't taste good
Octopuses can feel things like pleasure and pain
Octopus farms would be far too expensive to run
Octopuses carry diseases
questions.why: Beth explains the objection: octopuses are sentient – they experience feelings.

questions.q: According to Claire Marshall, why haven't octopuses been farmed before?
options: It was against the law everywhere
They have a complex life cycle and are hard to keep
Nobody wanted to eat them
They grow much too slowly to be sold at a profit in shops
questions.why: She says they have an incredibly complex life cycle, need live food and are solitary.

questions.q: Why is it a problem that octopuses are solitary?
options: They attack farmers
They stop eating
They are able to escape from their tanks much more easily
It is hard to keep many of them together in captivity
questions.why: Unlike chickens and pigs, they like to live alone, making captivity difficult because of space.

questions.q: What did Dr Heather Browning's research find?
options: Octopuses have no brain
Octopuses feel much less pain than fish or birds do
Octopuses met many of the signs of sentience
Octopuses can't learn anything
questions.why: She says octopuses seemed to meet many of the criteria they laid out.

questions.q: What does Beth suggest at the end of the discussion?
options: The argument about farming octopus will go on
Octopus farming has been banned
Everyone now agrees octopus farming is fine
Scientists have stopped studying octopuses completely
questions.why: She says the debate about whether it's OK to farm and eat octopuses will continue.
